en: Points of Controversy The Great Fifty-Section The Seventh Chapter
The Discourse on Aging and Death as Ripening:
Is aging and death ripening? Yes.
To be experienced as pleasant, to be experienced as painful, to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant;
associated with pleasant feeling, associated with painful feeling, associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
associated with contact, associated with feeling, associated with perception, associated with volition, associated with consciousness; having an object.
Is there for it turning toward, mental engagement, attention, volition, aspiration, and resolve?
One should not say so... [etc. ...
Is it not rather neither to be experienced as pleasant nor to be experienced as painful... [etc. ... and without an object?
Is there no turning back for him … nor any aspiration?
Yes. If it is neither to be experienced as pleasure nor to be experienced as pain … nor has it any object; [then it follows that there is no turning back, etc.]? Yes.
There is for him no turning back... nor aspiration. Yet, indeed, it should not be said:
"Aging-and-death is karmic fruition.
Contact is karmic fruition; contact is to be experienced as pleasant, contact is to be experienced as painful... [and so forth].
It has an object;
does it have turning toward [the object]... up to ...
aspiration? Yes.
Is aging-and-death a result? Is aging-and-death to be experienced as pleasant, to be experienced as painful, [and so on] … up to … has it an object?
Is there for it turning away … up to … aspiration?
It should not be said thus ...
[as before] ... Is aging-and-death a result? Is aging-and-death neither to be experienced as pleasant nor to be experienced as painful? ... [as before] ... Is it without an object?
Is there no turning toward it ... [as before] ... nor aspiration for it?
“Yes.
“Contact is a result (vipāka). Contact is neither to be experienced as pleasant nor to be experienced as painful … [and so on] … it is without an object;
there is for it no turning toward … [and so on] … no aspiration?”
It should not be stated thus… [as before] …Is the aging-and-death of unwholesome states the result of unwholesome states? Yes.
Is the aging-and-death of wholesome states the result of wholesome states?
One should not say so… [as before] … The aging-and-death of wholesome states; it should not be said that it is the result of wholesome states.
“Is it the result of wholesome states?
Yes. Is the aging and death of unwholesome states not to be so described? Yes.
“Is it the ripening of unwholesome states?
One should not say so… [as before]… Is aging-and-death the ripening of wholesome states, and the ripening of unwholesome states?
“Yes,” you say.
“Is the aging and death of unwholesome states the result of wholesome states?
You should not say so… [and so on].
Is the aging and death of unwholesome states not to be called the result of wholesome states? Yes.
Is the aging and death of wholesome states not to be called "the result of unwholesome states"?
It should not be so stated… [and so on].
Is the aging and death of both wholesome and unwholesome phenomena the result (vipāka) of unwholesome phenomena?
Yes. Is the aging and death of both wholesome and unwholesome phenomena the result of wholesome phenomena? No.
It should not be said so...
[and so on] ...Is it not the case that the aging and death of both wholesome and unwholesome phenomena should not be called "the result of wholesome phenomena"?
“Yes.
[The opponent asks: “Is the aging and death of both wholesome and unwholesome phenomena not to be called ‘the result of unwholesome phenomena’?”
It should not be said so … [as before] … Should it not be said that “aging-and-death is kamma-result”?
“Yes.
“But is there not karma that leads to ugliness and karma that leads to a short life?
“Yes.”
If there is indeed karma leading to ugliness and karma leading to a short lifespan, then indeed, O sir, it should be said:
"Old age and death are a result.
The discussion on whether old age and death are a result is finished.
